title: CREATE PROCEDURE and CALL
description: A PROCEDURE is like a FUNCTION but it's meant to perform actions (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) rather than compute and return a value - you invoke it with CALL instead of using it inside a SELECT. Create a procedure `give_department_raise(dept_id INTEGER, amount NUMERIC)` that adds `amount` to the salary of every employee in department `dept_id`. Then CALL it to give department 1 (Engineering) a $500 raise.
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: CREATE PROCEDURE, CALL
CREATE PROCEDURE <name>(<params>) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN <body>; END; $$ - no RETURNS clause at all, since a procedure doesn't hand back a value the way a function does.
The body is a single UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + amount WHERE department_id = dept_id; then, as a separate statement, CALL give_department_raise(1, 500).
expected_behavior: Every Engineering (department 1) employee's salary increases by exactly 500; every other department is untouched.
solution: CREATE PROCEDURE give_department_raise(dept_id INTEGER, amount NUMERIC) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + amount WHERE department_id = dept_id; END; $$; CALL give_department_raise(1, 500);
explanation: The FUNCTION vs PROCEDURE split exists because a function is meant to be usable inside a query expression (SELECT my_func(...)) - a procedure isn't, since its whole point is to run statements that change data, which CALL reflects by being its own top-level statement rather than something you SELECT.
postgres_note: PROCEDURE support (and CALL) was added in Postgres 11 - before that, everything (side effects included) had to be written as a FUNCTION.
